opus-5.5.text:
I think reinforcement learning is really the key ingredient that lets us move beyond imitation. Pre-training on internet-scale data is incredibly powerful, but at its core it's teaching a model to predict what a human would write. That gets you a remarkably capable system, but it's anchored to the distribution of human-generated text. If all you ever do is imitate, you're bounded, roughly, by the quality of the data you're imitating.

RL changes the objective. Instead of "what would a person say here," the question becomes "what actually works?" If you can define a signal for success, like whether a proof checks, whether code passes its tests, or whether an answer to a hard math problem is correct, the model can explore, try many approaches, and get reinforced for the ones that succeed, even if no human ever wrote down that exact path. That's where you start to see behavior that isn't just a compressed copy of human reasoning but something discovered.

We've seen this before in narrower domains. AlphaGo is the classic example. It started by learning from human games, but self-play and RL took it well past the best human players and produced moves that experts initially thought were mistakes. The exciting thing now is that we have pre-trained language models as a very general starting point, so we can apply that same recipe of strong prior plus RL across a much broader range of tasks.

Reasoning is where this has been most striking. When you train models with RL to think before they answer, to spend more compute at test time working through a problem, you see them learn to backtrack, check their work, and try alternative strategies. Nobody hand-coded those behaviors. They emerged because they lead to correct answers more often. And you get this nice scaling property: more RL compute and more thinking time keep improving performance.

That said, I'd be careful not to overstate it. The big open challenge is reward. In math and code we have fairly crisp verifiers, but much of what we care about, like good research taste, sound judgment in open-ended situations, or writing something genuinely insightful, doesn't come with a clean pass/fail signal. How we extend RL into those fuzzier domains, whether through learned reward models, models critiquing models, or richer environments, is probably one of the most important research questions right now. There are also real safety considerations: optimizing hard against an imperfect reward invites reward hacking, so you need to be thoughtful about what you're optimizing.

But directionally, I'm quite optimistic. Pre-training gives you breadth and a rich world model. RL gives you the ability to push past the frontier of the data. Together, I think that's the most credible path we have toward systems that don't just match human capabilities in important areas but exceed them.

r001.rationale: The response presents reinforcement learning as the key to moving beyond imitation and says models can discover new approaches and behaviors that improve success, supporting their ability to exceed human capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest framing is that pretraining on its own has a kind of ceiling built into it. If you train a model to predict the next token of what humans have written, the thing you're asymptoting toward is a very good imitation of the distribution of human output. You might get something that's broader than any single person, because it's seen everything, but the target is still fundamentally "what would a person have written here." And there's no reason that should carry you past the people who generated the data.

Reinforcement learning changes the target. Instead of asking "does this look like what a human would say," you're asking "did this actually work." Did the proof check out, did the code pass the tests, did the answer turn out to be correct. And once the signal is grounded in outcomes rather than in imitation, the model is free to find strategies that no human put in the training data. That's really the whole story of AlphaGo and then AlphaZero. The version that learned from human games was strong, but the version that learned purely from self-play, with nothing but the win condition as feedback, found moves that professionals initially thought were mistakes and turned out to be better.

What I find exciting about the current moment is that we're seeing the same dynamic show up in reasoning. When you let a model think for a long time and reward it for getting to the right answer, it starts to develop behaviors you didn't explicitly teach. It checks its own work, it backtracks, it tries a second approach when the first one stalls. Nobody wrote a curriculum for that. It emerges because those behaviors are what actually lead to correct answers, and the optimizer finds them.

Now, the caveat I'd give is that this only works as far as you can verify. Math and code are the easy cases because the reward is clean. The harder and more interesting frontier is domains where the signal is noisier, where it's a judgment call whether something was good. I think a lot of the progress over the next few years is going to come from getting better at constructing those reward signals, including using models themselves to evaluate, so that the loop can run in places where you don't have a compiler telling you yes or no.

But if you ask me where superhuman capability comes from, mechanically, it's that loop. Attempt, get feedback from reality, update, repeat, with the model generating its own experience rather than consuming ours. Pretraining gets you to the frontier of human knowledge. RL is how you step past it.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning lets models develop behaviors they were not explicitly taught and find strategies absent from human training data, enabling them to move beyond human capability.

astra-6.text:
I think reinforcement learning is a really important part of that story. When you train a model to imitate human text, you give it an incredibly rich starting point. But the training signal is essentially, “What would a human say here?” And that’s different from asking, “What action would actually lead to the best outcome?”

Reinforcement learning gives you a way to optimize for that second question. A model can try to solve a problem, get feedback on whether its solution worked, and improve. It doesn’t necessarily need a human to demonstrate a better solution. If it can discover one and recognize that it’s better, it can learn from it.

Games are a clear illustration of this: you can have a very simple signal about winning or losing, and that can drive the discovery of strategies that humans wouldn’t have taught the system. With language models, coding and mathematics offer some of that same opportunity, because you can often check an answer even when producing it is very difficult.

The harder question is how broadly we can make that work. In a lot of real-world tasks, success is ambiguous, feedback is delayed, and a reward can accidentally encourage the wrong behavior. So I wouldn’t say reinforcement learning automatically gets us there. But learning from the outcomes of your own attempts, rather than only from existing human examples, seems like a very powerful route to exceeding human performance.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning can help models discover strategies and improve beyond human performance, but describes it as a powerful route rather than stating that surpassing humans at critical tasks requires acquiring new skills during reinforcement learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reinforcement learning is a really important part of that story, because imitation alone gives you a somewhat indirect objective. You’re learning to predict what a human would say or do, whereas ultimately we want systems that can figure out what actually works.

With reinforcement learning, a model can try something, get feedback, and improve. And in domains where you can reliably evaluate the outcome—whether a program passes its tests, for example—there’s no inherent reason that process has to stop at human performance. The system can discover strategies that weren’t present in its training examples.

The challenge is getting the feedback right. For many of the things we care about, success is much harder to measure than winning a game. So I’d expect progress to be uneven: potentially very strong in areas with clear, verifiable rewards, and more difficult where judging the outcome itself requires expertise or involves ambiguous human preferences.

r001.rationale: The response says reinforcement learning can discover strategies absent from training examples and may exceed human performance, but it does not state that surpassing humans at critical tasks requires acquiring new skills during reinforcement learning.
